generatedProse.concept-context: In your subject, the aim is to understand, not just to get an answer on the screen. These eight techniques all put you to work: you explain ideas back, get questioned, practise, map what connects, and test your own reasoning. The tool supports the effort; it never does the understanding for you. Pick the technique that fits what you are trying to learn.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students preparing the same hard topic for a seminar.

{{learner-a}} asks the tool to summarise the topic and reads the summary twice. It all makes sense on the page. In the seminar, asked to explain the idea without notes, {{learner-a}} cannot do it. The tool had done the understanding, and none of it had moved across.

{{learner-b}} uses two techniques. First, explain it back: {{learner-b}} reads the tool's explanation, closes it, writes the idea from memory, then asks what was missed. Second, a Socratic turn: {{learner-b}} asks the tool to question the explanation one step at a time. The gaps show up, and {{learner-b}} can hold the idea with no tool open.

Both used the same tool on the same topic. Only {{learner-b}} used it to build understanding, not to replace it.
generatedProse.summary: Deep learning comes from doing the work, with the tool as a partner. Explaining back, Socratic questioning, targeted practice, feedback on your own work, mapping ideas, playing devil's advocate, learning by analogy, and preparing to read all share one move: you think, and the tool helps. You can now match a technique to what you want to learn and build a short routine from them. The last lesson brings the framework, the moves and the techniques together.

check.body: In the worked example, why could the second student explain the idea with no tool open?

items.text: They used techniques that made them do the thinking, such as explaining it back and being questioned.
They read the tool's summary more carefully than the first student.
They used a tool that gives more detailed summaries.
They memorised the tool's exact wording.

feedback.correct: That's right. Explaining back and Socratic questioning build understanding you keep, because you do the work.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what the second student did that forced their own thinking.
feedback.incorrectFinal: The second student explained the idea back and let the tool question them, so the understanding was theirs. Re-reading, a better tool, or memorising wording would not build it.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
